claim: Nectochaete larvae of Platynereis dumerilii are planktonic and swim with beating cilia arranged into segmental bands (trochs).
source: Nectochaete larvae of the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii are planktonic and swim with beating cilia arranged into segmental bands (trochs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the larval morphology.

claim: The Platynereis larva has three main trunk segments, each with two pairs of parapodia endowed with spiny chaetae and a complex musculature.
source: The larva has three main trunk segments, each with two pairs of parapodia endowed with spiny chaetae and a complex musculature (Fischer et al., 2010).
evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Fischer et al., 2010.

claim: Upon disturbances to the surrounding water, freely swimming Platynereis larvae abruptly stop swimming, contract the body and simultaneously elevate parapodia in all segments and on both sides of the body.
source: Upon disturbances to the surrounding water, freely swimming larvae abruptly stop swimming, contract the body and simultaneously elevate parapodia in all segments and on both sides of the body (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This behavioral observation is directly stated and supported by Figure 1B-C showing the response.

claim: The startle response in Platynereis larvae is followed by a slower recovery phase.
source: This response is followed by a slower recovery phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by reference to supplementary figures and video.

claim: When stimulated from the anterior, Platynereis larvae closed their beating cilia and elevated the parapodia.
source: When we stimulated larvae from the anterior, they closed their beating cilia and elevated the parapodia.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results described in the text.

claim: Both ciliary closure and parapodial elevation aspects of the startle response were modulated as a function of filament speed.
source: Both aspects of the response were modulated as a function of filament speed (Figure 1G).
evidence: This relationship is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The main ciliary band (prototroch) closed in all trials except at the lowest filament speeds tested.
source: The main ciliary band (prototroch) closed in all trials except at the lowest filament speeds tested (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The closures of ciliary bands extended to all locomotor ciliary bands (bodytrochs).
source: The closures extended to all locomotor ciliary bands (hereafter referred to as bodytrochs) (Video 2).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Video 2.

claim: Parapodial elevation was triggered with some of the lowest filament speeds tested, but was only consistently observed above 28 µm/ms.
source: Although parapodial elevation was triggered with some of the lowest filament speeds tested, it was only consistently observed above 28 µm/ms.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: The extent of parapodial elevation was dependent on the speed of the filament and displayed a bimodal distribution.
source: The extent of the elevation of parapodia was dependent on the speed of the filament and displayed a bimodal distribution (Figure 1G).
evidence: This relationship is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The parapodial elevation distribution was split into low-angle and wide-angle elevation responses (LowE and WideE, respectively) by a cutoff obtained from adjusting the data to a finite mixture model.
source: We split the distribution into low-angle and wide-angle elevation responses (LowE and WideE, respectively) by a cutoff obtained from adjusting the data to a finite mixture model (Figure 1E–G, Video 2).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described in the text and supported by figures and video.

claim: LowE responses were more common at low to moderate filament speeds, while WideE responses were seen across a broad stimulus-intensity spectrum.
source: LowE responses were more common at low to moderate speeds, while WideE responses were seen across a broad stimulus-intensity spectrum (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by the referenced figures.

claim: WideE responses had a shorter latency than LowE responses.
source: WideE responses had a shorter latency and the maximum parapodial elevation was achieved sooner than LowE responses (Figure 1J, and data not shown).
evidence: This temporal difference is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1J.

claim: Ciliary arrests and WideE responses occurred in close succession to each other.
source: Ciliary arrests and WideE responses occurred in close succession to each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This temporal relationship is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: As the filament was moved further away from the head, the response profile shifted to greater filament speeds.
source: As we moved the filament further away from the head, the response profile shifted to greater filament speeds (Figure 1I), showing that the response is triggered by near-field hydrodynamic disturbances.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1I, with an interpretation provided.

claim: The startle response is triggered by near-field hydrodynamic disturbances.
source: As we moved the filament further away from the head, the response profile shifted to greater filament speeds (Figure 1I), showing that the response is triggered by near-field hydrodynamic disturbances.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the distance-dependent response profile shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Posterior stimulation triggered startle behaviours with a markedly different response profile compared to anterior stimuli.
source: Next, we stimulated larvae from the posterior end (pygidium) from a 100 μm distance. Posterior stimulation triggered startle behaviours with a markedly different response profile compared to anterior stimuli (Figure 1H).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1H.

claim: Animals were less sensitive to posterior stimulation as only filament speeds >19 μm/ms triggered a response.
source: First, animals were less sensitive to posterior stimulation as only filament speeds >19 μm/ms triggered a response.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data comparing anterior and posterior stimulation.

claim: Upon posterior stimulation, only WideE and no LowE responses were observed.
source: Second, we only observed WideE and no LowE responses.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the posterior stimulation experiments.

claim: WideE responses upon posterior stimulation were often not accompanied by ciliary closures.
source: The WideE responses were often not accompanied by ciliary closures.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the posterior stimulation experiments.

claim: Prototroch ciliary closures not accompanied by a WideE response were only very rarely observed.
source: On the contrary, we only very rarely observed (prototroch) ciliary closures not accompanied by a WideE response.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: WideE responses triggered from anterior and posterior stimulation had similar latencies (anterior: 31.7 ms median; posterior: 42 ms median).
source: WideE responses triggered from anterior and posterior stimulation were similarly fast (anterior and posterior WideE response median latency: 31.7 ms and 42 ms, respectively)(Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: Ciliary closures had median latencies of 65 ms for prototroch and 45.6 ms for bodytrochs.
source: WideE responses accompanied by prototroch ciliary closures were temporarily uncoupled (ciliary closures median latency: 65 ms (prototroch) or 45.6 ms (bodytrochs);) (Figure 1J, K).
evidence: These quantitative measurements are stated in the text and supported by Figure 1J, K.

claim: During WideE responses the three chaeta-bearing segments and the left and right body sides were highly coordinated.
source: During WideE responses the three chaeta-bearing segments and the left and right body sides were highly coordinated.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The extent of parapodial elevation was bilaterally symmetric in all responses observed.
source: As already apparent from freely swimming larvae (Figure 1C) the extent of the elevation was bilaterally symmetric in all responses observed (Figure 1F shows a representative example).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figures 1C and 1F.

claim: The delay values between the onset of elevation of the first pair of left and right parapodia were mostly below the recording speed limit.
source: The delay values between the onset of elevation of the first pair of left and right parapodia were mostly below our recording speed limit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This temporal measurement is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: Parapodia in different segments, but on the same body side rose simultaneously or one frame apart from each other.
source: Parapodia in different segments, but on the same body side rose simultaneously or one frame apart from each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This temporal observation is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: The startle response in Platynereis larvae is rapid, left-right symmetric, segmentally coordinated, and stereotypical.
source: We thus characterized a rapid, left-right symmetric, segmentally coordinated, stereotypical whole-body startle response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental observations described.

claim: The startle response is triggered by hydrodynamic stimuli and has a scalable profile that is different depending on the direction of stimulus.
source: The response is triggered by hydrodynamic stimuli and has a scalable profile that is different depending on the direction of stimulus.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental observations comparing anterior and posterior stimulation.

claim: The most likely candidates to sense flow-driven strain and bending are neurons with ciliary structures penetrating the cuticular surface.
source: The most likely candidates to sense flow-driven strain and bending are neurons with ciliary structures penetrating the cuticular surface (Budelmann, 1989).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on established knowledge cited from Budelmann, 1989.

claim: All penetrating uniciliated, biciliated and multiciliated sensory neurons were identified and mapped across the whole body of nectochaete larvae using SEM and ssTEM.
source: Using a combination of scanning (SEM) and ssTEM, we identified and mapped all penetrating uniciliated, biciliated and multiciliated sensory neurons across the whole body of nectochaete larvae (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This methodological approach and result is stated in the text and supported by the figures.

claim: Nectochaete larvae have a stereotypical morphology, allowing the same cells to be reliably identified in different larvae by SEM and in the ssTEM dataset.
source: Since nectochaete larvae have a stereotypical morphology, the same cells could be reliably identified in different larvae by SEM and in the ssTEM dataset (Randel et al., 2015).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Randel et al., 2015.

claim: CR neurons in Platynereis have a single non-motile cilium with a 9 × 2 + 2 microtubule doublet pattern and a symmetric collar of 10 thick microvilli surrounding the cilium.
source: The CR neurons in Platynereis have a single non-motile cilium with a 9 × 2 + 2 microtubule doublet pattern and a symmetric collar of 10 thick microvilli surrounding the cilium (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This structural description is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C-D.

claim: Each microvillus in CR neurons has a dense region in the inner side and is connected by thin fibres to the cilium.
source: Each microvillus has a dense region in the inner side and is connected by thin fibres to the cilium (Figure 2D).
evidence: This structural detail is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The collar and the cilium of CR neurons penetrate the cuticle, allowing these cells to be identified in SEM samples.
source: The collar and the cilium penetrate the cuticle, thus these cells can also be identified in SEM samples (Figure 2C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: CR neurons occur in other regions of the nectochaete larva, either individually or in clusters as parts of developing organs.
source: CR neurons also occur in other regions of the nectochaete larva, either individually or in clusters as parts of developing organs (Figure 2A,B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This distribution pattern is stated in the text and supported by the figures.

claim: When larvae were stimulated with a vibrating filament, the cilia of the hCR1 cells deflected and GCaMP6s fluorescence increased in the cell bodies and in the cilia.
source: When we stimulated larvae with a vibrating filament, the cilia of the hCR1 cells deflected and GCaMP6s fluorescence increased in the cell bodies and in the cilia (Figure 2E–G, Video 5 and Video 6).
evidence: This experimental observation is stated in the text and supported by figures and videos.

claim: Although the cilium of MS1 was deflected by the stimulus, the fluorescence did not increase in this cell.
source: Although the cilium of MS1 was also deflected, the fluorescence did not increase in this cell (Figure 2G, and Video 6).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2G and Video 6.

claim: hCR2 neurons were activated by the hydrodynamic stimulus.
source: hCR2 neurons were also activated by the stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: Head CR neurons detect hydrodynamic vibrations and could trigger the startle response.
source: These results show that head CR neurons detect hydrodynamic vibrations and could thus trigger the startle response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calcium imaging experiments showing CR neuron activation.

claim: A Platynereis ortholog of the TRPP/Polycystin-2 channel, PKD2-1, was expressed in CR neurons.
source: We found that a Platynereis ortholog of the TRPP/Polycystin-2 channel, PKD2-1, (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) was expressed in CR neurons, as demonstrated by in situ hybridization and a transgenic reporter construct (Figure 3A,B,D).
evidence: This expression pattern is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures showing in situ hybridization and reporter expression.

claim: PKD2-1 was expressed in two other types of penetrating uni- and biciliated sensory neurons (PU and PB neurons, respectively) in the head, trunk, and pygidium.
source: PKD2-1 was also expressed in two other types of penetrating uni- and biciliated sensory neurons (PU and PB neurons, respectively) in the head, trunk, and pygidium, including an unpaired biciliated sensory cell in the pygidium (pygPBunp) (formerly pygPBbicil;Shahidi et al., 2015; Verasztó et al., 2017)(Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This expression pattern is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure and citations.

claim: PKD1-1 was expressed only in CR neurons and in the pygPBunp neuron at the nectochaete stage.
source: Another gene in Platynereis, PKD1-1, was expressed only in CR neurons and in the pygPBunpneuron at the nectochaete stage (Figure 3A,C,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Video 7).
evidence: This expression pattern is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures and video.

claim: PKD1-1 belongs to the TRPP-related family PKD1, and it defines a novel invertebrate family that is paralogous to the more widespread Polycystin-1 and PKD1L1 families.
source: PKD1-1 belongs to the TRPP-related family PKD1, and it defines a novel invertebrate family that is paralogous to the more widespread Polycystin-1 and PKD1L1 families (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This phylogenetic classification is stated in the text and supported by the phylogenetic tree in the supplementary figure.

claim: Homozygote and trans-heterozygote larvae for either PKD1-1 or PKD2-1 alleles were viable and fertile and had normal CR neuron morphology.
source: Homozygote and trans-heterozygote larvae for either PKD1-1 or PKD2-1 alleles were viable and fertile and had normal CR neuron morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure showing normal morphology.

claim: PKD1-1 and PKD2-1 mutant larvae failed to startle upon touching their head, a stimulus that triggered the startle response in most wild type and heterozygote larvae.
source: These larvae, however, failed to startle upon touching their head, a stimulus that triggered the startle response in most wild type and heterozygote larvae (Figure 4E–F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This behavioral phenotype is stated in the text and supported by the figure and source data.

claim: The neuronal expression of PKD1-1 and PKD2-1 channels is essential for the hydrodynamic startle response in Platynereis larvae.
source: This demonstrates that the neuronal expression of PKD1-1 and PKD2-1 channels is essential for the hydrodynamic startle response in Platynereis larvae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant phenotype data showing complete loss of the startle response.

claim: In most experiments, PKD2-1mut/mut larvae were predated more than their wildtype counterparts (p < 0.001).
source: In most experiments, PKD2-1mut/mut larvae were predated more than their wildtype counterparts (p < 0.001, one-sided exact Wilcoxon-Pratt signed rank test, Figure 5B).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the text with the specific test used and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Wild type but not mutant larvae showed the startle response upon copepod attacks.
source: As wild type but not mutant larvae showed the startle response upon copepod attacks (Video 9), the difference in predation rates is likely due to the absence of a startle response in PKD2-1mut/mut larvae.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Video 9.

claim: The difference in predation rates between wild type and PKD2-1mut/mut larvae is likely due to the absence of a startle response in PKD2-1mut/mut larvae.
source: As wild type but not mutant larvae showed the startle response upon copepod attacks (Video 9), the difference in predation rates is likely due to the absence of a startle response in PKD2-1mut/mut larvae.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed behavioral difference and predation data.

claim: The head and pygidial CRs project along the ventral nerve cord (VNC) posteriorly and anteriorly, respectively.
source: The head and pygidial CRs project along the ventral nerve cord (VNC) posteriorly and anteriorly, respectively (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and form en passant synapses with distinct types of interneurons (INs) and motoneurons (MNs) (Figure 6B–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the text and supported by the figures.

claim: CR neurons form en passant synapses with distinct types of interneurons (INs) and motoneurons (MNs).
source: The head and pygidial CRs project along the ventral nerve cord (VNC) posteriorly and anteriorly, respectively (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and form en passant synapses with distinct types of interneurons (INs) and motoneurons (MNs) (Figure 6B–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by the figures.

claim: CR interneurons target muscle-motor and ciliomotor neurons that innervate several muscle types and the ciliary bands in the larva on both body sides.
source: These INs in turn target muscle-motor and ciliomotor neurons that innervate several muscle types and the ciliary bands in the larva on both body sides (Figures 6–8).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6-8.

claim: The head CRs directly synapse on the MC cell, a previously described cholinergic motoneuron that induces ciliary closures of the prototroch ciliary band.
source: The head CRs directly synapse on the MC cell, a previously described cholinergic motoneuron that induces ciliary closures of the prototroch ciliary band (Verasztó et al., 2017) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text, supported by Figure 6B, and cited from previous work.

claim: The head but not the pygidial CRs synapse extensively on CM interneurons (INCM), a bilateral pair of ipsilaterally projecting pseudo-unipolar neurons with a soma in the 1st segment.
source: The head but not the pygidial CRs also synapse extensively on CM interneurons (INCM), a bilateral pair of ipsilaterally projecting pseudo-unipolar neurons with a soma in the 1st segment (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6B-C.

claim: The CM interneurons are presynaptic to the Loop neurons on the same side and to MNant on both body sides.
source: The CMs are presynaptic to the Loop neurons on the same side and to MNant on both body sides (Figure 6B and Figure 8).
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6B and 8.

claim: Loop and MNant are ciliomotor neurons that likely control the closures of prototroch and bodytroch cilia.
source: Loop and MNant are ciliomotor neurons that likely control the closures of prototroch and bodytroch cilia (Verasztó et al., 2017)(Figure 6B).
evidence: This functional interpretation is stated in the text, supported by Figure 6B, and cited from previous work.

claim: Head CRs synapse on Rope interneurons (INrope), which have their soma in the head and have ipsilateral descending projections that span the entire VNC.
source: Head CRs also synapse on a novel interneuron type, the Rope interneurons (INrope). These neurons have their soma in the head and have ipsilateral descending projections that span the entire VNC (Figure 6C).
evidence: This connectivity and anatomy is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: INrope neurons make synaptic contacts with the Loop neurons, providing a converging pathway to ciliary control.
source: INrope neurons make synaptic contacts with the Loop neurons (Figure 6B), thus providing a converging pathway to ciliary control.
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6B, with an interpretation of its functional significance.

claim: Both head and pygidial CRs target the sensory-motor neuron pygPBunp, which may modulate the prototroch ciliary band system.
source: Finally, both head and pygidial CRs target the sensory-motor neuron pygPBunp, which may modulate the prototroch ciliary band system (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text and cited from previous work, with a functional interpretation.

claim: Both head and pygidial CRs directly synapse on the Crab motoneurons (MNcrab), a unique set of decussating VNC motoneurons that innervate a variety of trunk muscles.
source: CRs also feed into distinct muscle-motor pathways (Figure 6B). Both head and pygidial CRs directly synapse on the Crab motoneurons (MNcrab), a unique set of decussating VNC motoneurons that innervate a variety of trunk muscles (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures.

claim: The descending projections of Rope neurons target several segmentally arranged ipsi- and contralaterally projecting VNC motoneurons (MNvnc) that innervate distinct sets of somatic muscles in all three segments and on both body sides.
source: The descending projections of Rope neurons target several segmentally arranged ipsi- and contralaterally projecting VNC motoneurons (MNvnc) that innervate distinct sets of somatic muscles (longitudinal, oblique, transverse, and parapodial groups) in all three segments and on both body sides (Figure 7A–C, Figure 8, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures.

claim: Split interneurons (INsplit) are a group of segmentally arranged ipsilateral pseudounipolar cells similar in morphology to CMs.
source: An alternative muscle-motor pathway is through the Split interneurons (INsplit), a group of segmentally arranged ipsilateral pseudounipolar cells (similar in morphology to CMs) (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1,Video 10).
evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the text and supported by the figures and video.

claim: INsplit neurons synapse onto numerous ipsi- and contralaterally projecting MNvnc neurons in all segments, some of which are also targeted by INrope.
source: INsplit neurons synapse onto numerous ipsi- and contralaterally projecting MNvnc neurons in all segments (Figure 7A and Figure 8), some of these MNs are also targeted by INrope (see Venn diagram in Figure 7A; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures.

claim: INsplit cells are postsynaptic to head, trunk and pygidial CRs.
source: INsplit cells are postsynaptic to head, trunk and pygidial CRs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6B.

claim: CRs synapse on a heterogenous group of ascending and descending trunk commissural interneurons (INcomm).
source: CRs also synapse on a heterogenous group of ascending and descending trunk commissural interneurons (INcomm) (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This connectivity is stated in the text and supported by the figures.

claim: Bilateral pairs of INcomm targeted by left and right CRs could not be found.
source: In contrast to the other interneuron types, we could not find bilateral pairs of INcomm targeted by left and right CRs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: Some commissural neurons synapse on contralateral interneurons and motoneurons in the startle network and also feed back to the CRs.
source: Some of these commissural neurons synapse on contralateral interneurons and motoneurons in the startle network and also feed back to the CRs (Figure 6B and Figure 8).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6B and 8.

claim: The majority of motoneurons targeted by INcomm are also targeted by INsplit and INrope.
source: The majority of motoneurons targeted by INcomm are also targeted by INsplit and INrope (see Venn diagram in Figure 7A).
evidence: This connectivity overlap is stated in the text and shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 7A.

claim: The VNC motoneurons targeted by INsplit, INrope and INcomm belong to at least ten morphologically distinct groups, with segmentally iterated and left-right symmetric members.
source: The VNC motoneurons targeted by INsplit, INrope and INcomm belong to at least ten morphologically distinct groups, with segmentally iterated and left-right symmetric members (Figure 7A,B, Figure 8, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This classification is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures.

claim: The contralateral motoneurons MNcrab, MNring, MNspider and MNsmile innervate all the distinct muscle classes involved in the startle response and account for most of the synaptic targets on muscles.
source: The contralateral motoneurons MNcrab, MNring, MNspider and MNsmile innervate all the distinct muscle classes involved in the startle response (longitudinal, oblique, transverse, axochord and parapodial groups) and account for most of the synaptic targets on muscles.
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text.

claim: Ipsilateral neurons target exclusively oblique and parapodial muscles.
source: Ipsilateral neurons target exclusively oblique and parapodial muscles (Figure 8, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This connectivity pattern is stated in the text and supported by the figures.

claim: MNbow is a motoneuron class with both ipsilateral and decussating axonal projections that targets exclusively oblique and parapodial muscles.
source: This is also true for MNbow, a motoneuron class with both ipsilateral and decussating axonal projections Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure.

claim: Calcium imaging during startle responses directly confirmed the contraction of the longitudinal, oblique, axochord and parapodial muscle groups.
source: By calcium imaging during startle responses, we could directly confirm the contraction of the longitudinal, oblique, axochord and parapodial muscle groups (Figure 7C and Video 11).
evidence: This experimental observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7C and Video 11.

claim: CR neurons are similar to collar receptor cells (CRs) previously identified in other polychaetes, earthworms and leeches.
source: We focused on penetrating ciliated sensory neurons on the head of the animal, as this region was the most sensitive to mechanosensory stimuli (Figure 1). We found different candidate cell types (Figure 2A–B), including a group of cells very similar to the collar receptor cells (CRs) previously identified in other polychaetes (Budelmann, 1989; Purschke, 2005; Purschke et al., 2017; Schlawny et al., 1991; Windoffer and Westheide, 1988), earthworms (Knapp and Mill, 1971) and leeches (Phillips and Friesen, 1982).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In leeches, CR-like cells (called 'S hairs') were suggested to be involved in the detection of water movement.
source: In leeches, these cells (called 'S hairs') were suggested to be involved in the detection of water movement (Friesen, 1981).
evidence: This functional suggestion is stated in the text and cited from Friesen, 1981.

claim: CR neurons are morphologically similar to hair cells in vertebrates, which also can detect water movement.
source: Morphologically, CR neurons are also similar to hair cells in vertebrates, which also can detect water movement (Engelmann et al., 2000).
evidence: This morphological comparison is stated in the text and cited from Engelmann et al., 2000.

claim: The normal morphology of the sensory ending of CR cells in PKD1-1 and PDK2-1 mutant animals suggests that PKD proteins are involved in the mechanotransduction cascade in Platynereis rather than having a structural role.
source: The normal morphology of the sensory ending of CR cells in PKD1-1 and PDK2-1 mutant animals suggests that PKD proteins are involved in the mechanotransduction cascade in Platynereis rather than having a structural role (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text and supported by the supplementary figure showing normal morphology.

claim: In zebrafish, the polycystin PKD2L1 is involved in mediating mechanotransduction in a neuronal context.
source: In zebrafish, the polycystin PKD2L1 is involved in mediating mechanotransduction in a neuronal context.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from zebrafish studies.

claim: PKD2L1 is expressed in cerebrospinal-fluid-contacting neurons in zebrafish and is required for the detection of tail bending by these neurons and for normal tail movements.
source: PKD2L1 is expressed in cerebrospinal-fluid-contacting neurons and is required for the detection of tail bending by these neurons and for normal tail movements (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: This functional role is stated in the text and cited from Böhm et al., 2016.

claim: In C. elegans, PKD2 and LOV-1 (a PKD1 paralog) are known to be required for neuronal mechanosensory function.
source: In C. elegans, PKD2 and LOV-1 (a PKD1 paralog) are known to be required for neuronal mechanosensory function (Barr and Sternberg, 1999).
evidence: This functional requirement is stated in the text and cited from Barr and Sternberg, 1999.

claim: Calcium signalling is not impaired in mechanosensory neurons in the C. elegans PKD2 mutant.
source: Despite this requirement, calcium signalling is not impaired in mechanosensory neurons in the C. elegans PKD2 mutant (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The startle response in Platynereis larvae consists of the fast and synchronous activation of specific muscles and the arrest of all locomotor cilia.
source: The startle response in Platynereis larvae consists of the fast and synchronous activation of specific muscles and the arrest of all locomotor cilia.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral observations.

claim: The startle response was absent in larvae mutant for PKD1-1 and PKD2-1.
source: These responses were absent in larvae mutant for PKD1-1 and PKD2-1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mutant phenotype.

claim: Mechanosensation is thought to be especially important for predator-prey interactions at small scales.
source: Mechanosensation is thought to be especially important for predator-prey interactions at small scales (Andersen et al., 2016; Martens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and cited from two references.

claim: Centropages typicus uses mechanoreceptors in its antennae to localize prey.
source: Platynereis larvae mutant for PKD2-1 would not stop swimming even at close distance from the copepod, which uses mechanoreceptors in its antennae to localize prey (Yen et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Yen et al., 1992.

claim: Slight disturbances in the surrounding medium could activate the CR neurons in the head of the larva to drive the closure of all locomotor cilia in a coordinated fashion.
source: We propose that slight disturbances in the surrounding medium activate the CR neurons in the head of the larva to drive the closure of all locomotor cilia in a coordinated fashion.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the circuit analysis.

claim: Ciliary closure could be driven by a feed-forward circuit from head CRs to the cholinergic MC neuron and the activation of the cholinergic Loop and MNant ciliomotor neurons via the CM interneurons.
source: This could be driven by a feed-forward circuit from head CRs to the cholinergic MC neuron and the activation of the cholinergic Loop and MNant ciliomotor neurons via the CM interneurons.
evidence: This is a proposed circuit mechanism based on the connectivity data.

claim: The beating of cilia generates a hydrodynamic signal that can be detected by predators at a distance.
source: The beating of cilia generates a hydrodynamic signal that can be detected by predators at a distance (Kiørboe and Visser, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Kiørboe and Visser, 1999.

claim: By shutting off cilia upon vibrations elicited by an approaching predator, the larva could avoid being detected.
source: By shutting off cilia upon vibrations elicited by an approaching predator, the larva could avoid being detected (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation supported by Figure 9A.

claim: The ability to cease ciliary beating upon mechanical stimulation has been reported in other ciliated larvae and could be a widespread predator avoidance mechanism.
source: The ability to cease ciliary beating upon mechanical stimulation has been reported in other ciliated larvae (Mackie et al., 1976) and could be a widespread predator avoidance mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and includes a speculation about its widespread nature.

claim: Rope neurons could simultaneously activate ciliomotor and trunk musclemotor neurons across all segments upon strong stimulation of head CRs.
source: The wiring diagram suggests that Rope neurons could simultaneously activate ciliomotor and trunk musclemotor neurons across all segments upon strong stimulation of head CRs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the wiring diagram analysis.

claim: Based on their anatomy and connectivity, Rope neurons are candidate command interneurons in Platynereis.
source: Thus, based on their anatomy and connectivity, Rope neurons are candidate command interneurons in Platynereis (Wiersma and Ikeda, 1964).
evidence: This is a proposed classification based on anatomical and connectivity data, with a citation to the concept of command neurons.

claim: The circuitry of Rope neurons resembles that of giant fibre systems in a variety of animals, such as the GF system in Drosophila, the lateral and medial giants in crayfish or the M cells in vertebrates.
source: Their circuitry resembles that of giant fibre systems in a variety of animals, such as the GF system in Drosophila, the lateral and medial giants in crayfish or the M cells in vertebrates (reviewed in Hale et al., 2016).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and cited from a review.

claim: Split interneurons constitute a second pathway for synchronous and intersegmental muscle contraction.
source: Beside the Rope neurons, Split interneurons constitute a second pathway for synchronous and intersegmental muscle contraction (Figure 6B, Figure 7A, and Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures.

claim: The Rope and Split systems could function in parallel to produce the complete startle response.
source: These two systems could function in parallel to produce the complete startle response (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the circuit analysis and supported by Figure 9C.

claim: A similar mechanism of parallel pathways has been suggested to be at work during whole-body shortening in the leech.
source: A similar mechanism has been suggested to be at work during whole-body shortening in the leech. Here, the fast-conducting S-cells trigger the initial muscle contraction followed by the activation of a slower pathway mediating extensive body shortening (Kristan et al., 2005; Shaw and Kristan, 1995).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and cited from two references.

claim: The Rope and Split pathways may implement different aspects of a startle behaviour depending on context or the nature, direction or intensity of the stimulus.
source: The Rope and Split pathways may also implement different aspects of a startle behaviour depending on context or the nature, direction or intensity of the stimulus (Fotowat et al., 2009; Kramer et al., 1981; Liu and Fetcho, 1999)(Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation based on the circuit analysis, with citations to similar phenomena in other organisms.

claim: The Split pathway may activate muscles independent of ciliary closures, as observed upon posterior stimulation.
source: For example, Split but not Rope neurons are also targeted by posterior CRs. This pathway may activate muscles independent of ciliary closures, as observed upon posterior stimulation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the connectivity data and behavioral observations.

claim: Such a response may help the larva to deter and escape a predator approaching from the posterior end.
source: Such a response may help the larva to deter and escape a predator approaching from the posterior end (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation supported by Figure 9D.

claim: Differences in connectivity of anterior and posterior sensory neurons to the downstream circuits have also been observed in C. elegans and crayfish.
source: Differences in connectivity of anterior and posterior sensory neurons to the downstream circuits have also been observed in C. elegans (Chalfie et al., 1985) and crayfish (Wine and Krasne, 1972).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and cited from two references.

claim: A hallmark of the startle response in Platynereis is its bilateral symmetry, both in timing and in the extent of muscle contraction.
source: A hallmark of the startle response in Platynereis is its bilateral symmetry, both in timing and in the extent of muscle contraction (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral observations supported by the figures.

claim: The proximity of the sensory cilia of all head and pygidial CRs suggests that both the left and right members are stimulated in most cases.
source: The proximity of the sensory cilia of all head and pygidial CRs suggests that both the left and right members are stimulated in most cases, as observed during calcium imaging of hCR1 cells (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations and supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Since the circuitry downstream of CR neurons is bilaterally symmetric, a coincident activation of left and right CRs would result in a synchronous response.
source: Since the circuitry downstream of CR neurons is bilaterally symmetric (Figure 8), a coincident activation of left and right CRs would result in a synchronous response.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the circuit symmetry shown in Figure 8.

claim: Ciliary coordination may partially rely on CM interneurons targeting ciliomotor MNant cells of both body sides.
source: Ciliary coordination may partially rely on CM interneurons targeting ciliomotor MNant cells of both body sides (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the connectivity data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Coincident left-right muscle contraction could be ensured by the connection of a single Rope neuron to both ipsi- and contralateral decussating motoneurons.
source: Coincident left-right muscle contraction could be ensured by the connection of a single Rope neuron to both ipsi- and contralateral decussating motoneurons.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the connectivity pattern.

claim: Split neurons have a similar bilateral connectivity pattern to Rope neurons.
source: Split neurons have a similar bilateral connectivity pattern (Figure 8).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8.

claim: A similar network motif of a single commissural interneuron innervating motoneurons on both body sides is present in the Drosophila larva.
source: A similar network motif is present in the Drosophila larva, where a single commissural interneuron innervates motoneurons on both body sides (Fushiki et al., 2016).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and cited from Fushiki et al., 2016.

claim: The commissural interneurons (INcomm) may contribute to left-right coordination.
source: The commissural interneurons (INcomm) may also contribute to left-right coordination.
evidence: This is a proposed function based on the connectivity pattern.

claim: In Drosophila, the amplitude of muscle contractions on both body sides is controlled by ascending commissural neurons.
source: In Drosophila, the amplitude of muscle contractions on both body sides is controlled by ascending commissural neurons (Heckscher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Heckscher et al., 2015.

claim: The evolutionary relationship of the Platynereis circuit to similar circuits in other bilaterians is currently unclear.
source: The evolutionary relationship of the Platynereis circuit to similar circuits in other bilaterians is currently unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Comparative connectomics of whole-body circuits has great potential to uncover circuit homologies.
source: Comparative connectomics of whole-body circuits has great potential to uncover circuit homologies.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential of a research approach.

claim: A recent analysis of the Ciona intestinalis larval connectome identified a putative startle circuit based on anatomy and connectivity alone that was suggested to be homologous to the Mauthner circuit of vertebrates.
source: A recent analysis of the Ciona intestinalis larval connectome identified a putative startle circuit based on anatomy and connectivity alone that was suggested to be homologous to the Mauthner circuit of vertebrates (Ryan et al., 2017; Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from two references.

claim: To understand circuit evolution, connectomics approaches will need to be complemented with genetic and behavioural experiments and the analysis of the constituent cell types.
source: To understand circuit evolution, such approaches will need to be complemented with genetic and behavioural experiments and the analysis of the constituent cell types.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for understanding circuit evolution.

claim: Only comparisons at different levels and at varying phylogenetic distances will allow us to reconstruct the evolution of circuits.
source: Only comparisons at these different levels and at varying phylogenetic distances will allow us to reconstruct the evolution of circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for studying circuit evolution.

claim: Startle responses triggered by aversive stimuli including predators are widespread across animals.
source: Startle responses triggered by aversive stimuli including predators are widespread across animals.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Startle responses require the rapid and simultaneous activation of a large number of muscles.
source: These coordinated whole-body actions require the rapid and simultaneous activation of a large number of muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a general characteristic of startle responses.

claim: Startle responses require the simultaneous activation of a large number of muscles in a coordinated manner with a short latency.
source: Startle responses require the simultaneous activation of a large number of muscles in a coordinated manner with a short latency (Eaton et al., 1977).
evidence: This is stated as a general characteristic and cited from Eaton et al., 1977.

claim: Startle responses are often achieved by a system of giant command neurons or motoneurons such as the giant fibres in crayfish, the Mauthner cells in fish and lampreys, or the giant motor axons in the jellyfish Aglantha digitale.
source: This is often achieved by a system of giant command neurons or motoneuron such as the giant fibres in crayfish (Wiersma and Ikeda, 1964), the Mauthner cells (M cells) in fish and lampreys (Korn and Faber, 2005) or the giant motor axons in the jellyfish Aglantha digitale (Roberts and Mackie, 1980).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Giant neurons increase transmission speed and accuracy, and enable activation of the locomotor system with the least number of intervening synapses.
source: Such giant neurons increase transmission speed and accuracy, and enable activation of the locomotor system with the least number of intervening synapses (Bullock, 1984).
evidence: This functional explanation is stated in the text and cited from Bullock, 1984.

claim: A common feature of startle circuits is the presence of converging neuronal pathways that activate the same effectors.
source: Another common feature of startle circuits is the presence of converging neuronal pathways that activate the same effectors.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of startle circuits.

claim: Convergence in startle circuits can contribute to behavioural flexibility.
source: This can contribute to behavioural flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as a functional consequence of circuit convergence.

claim: In crayfish, a non-giant circuitry is present that enables the animal to respond more variably to less abrupt stimuli.
source: In crayfish, a non-giant circuitry is present that enables the animal to respond more variably to less abrupt stimuli (Edwards et al., 1999; Kramer et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from two references.

claim: In fish, not only the M cell but also other descending reticulospinal neurons are required for short latency responses.
source: In fish, not only the M cell but also other descending reticulospinal neurons are required for short latency responses (Liu and Fetcho, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Liu and Fetcho, 1999.

claim: Convergence in startle circuits can occur at the sensory level, as shown in fish, crayfish and Drosophila larvae.
source: Convergence can also occur at the sensory level, as shown in fish, crayfish and Drosophila larvae (Lacoste et al., 2015; Ohyama et al., 2015; Zucker, 1972).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from three references.

claim: The motor programs during a startle response can differ depending on the location of the stimulus due to differences in connectivity downstream of different sensory fields.
source: The motor programs during a startle response can also differ depending on the location of the stimulus. This is due to differences in connectivity downstream of different sensory fields.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle with an explanation.

claim: In C. elegans and crayfish, partially overlapping circuits induce forward movement upon posterior stimulation, or backward movement upon anterior stimulation.
source: In C. elegans (Chalfie et al., 1985) and crayfish (Wine and Krasne, 1972), partially overlapping circuits induce forward movement upon posterior stimulation, or backward movement upon anterior stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from two references.

claim: In Drosophila larvae, backward or forward movement depends on stimulus direction, achieved by an interneuron type with differential connectivity in anterior and posterior segments.
source: In Drosophila larvae, backward or forward movement depends on stimulus direction. This is achieved by an interneuron type with differential connectivity in anterior and posterior segments (Takagi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Takagi et al., 2017.

claim: In C. elegans, defects in the touch response lead to a lower escape rate from fungal predators.
source: For example, in C. elegans, defects in the touch response lead to a lower escape rate from fungal predators (Maguire et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Maguire et al., 2011.

claim: Crayfish display giant-fibre-mediated tail flips to avoid approaching predators, but non-giant-mediated tail flips to escape following capture.
source: Crayfish display giant-fibre-mediated tail flips to avoid approaching predators, but non-giant-mediated tail flips to escape following capture (Herberholz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Herberholz et al., 2004.

claim: The study of the touch withdrawal response in C. elegans led to the discovery of key components of the mechanosensory cascade including the DEG/ENaC mechanotransduction channel complex MEC-4.
source: Here the study of the touch withdrawal response led to the discovery of key components of the mechanosensory cascade including the DEG/ENaC mechanotransduction channel complex MEC-4 (O'Hagan et al., 2005)(reviewed in Schafer, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from two references.

claim: Genetic and cell ablation techniques, combined with the analysis of the whole-body wiring diagram allowed the characterisation of the sensory-locomotor circuits involved in the touch withdrawal response in C. elegans.
source: Genetic and cell ablation techniques, combined with the analysis of the whole-body wiring diagram (White et al., 1986) allowed the characterisation of the sensory-locomotor circuits involved in the touch withdrawal response in C. elegans (Chalfie et al., 1985; Piggott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from three references.
